extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, political communicators, students of public_opinion and media
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and theoretical criteria for making news, fiction, cinema, and propaganda that will engage mass audiences and shape public opinion. Emphasizes visualization, identification, suspense, stereotypes, and the multifaceted nature of self-interest in reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial/visual value (visualization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea; an idea is not lucid for practical decision until it has visual or tactile value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical intelligence is closely adapted to spatial qualities; a "clear" thinker is often a good visualizer. Visualization can catch stimulus and result but may caricature intermediate or internal states; therefore, find gifted visualizers or render ideas into strong pictorial terms to make them usable in public decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy / identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea conveyed is not fully our own until we have identified ourselves with some aspect of the picture; Vernon Lee called this 'empathy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification can be subtle or symbolic and often operates unconsciously (mimicry). Effective representations supply 'handles' for identification so audiences can enter and feel the scene; without such handles, the message will feel like mist and fail to engage broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear marking of roles (recognizable hero/villain)
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation the handles for identification are almost always marked. You know who the hero is at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No work promises to be easily popular where the marking is not definite and the choice clear. Popular forms tend to mark heroes/antagonists clearly so audiences can immediately take sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience involvement / active exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must have something to do; contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful is not something to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid passive spectatorship, images/stories must allow audiences to exercise emotions and impulses (for example, through taking sides). News and fiction should create opportunities for audience activity (moral choice, rooting for outcome) to sustain attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary appeal motifs: sex and fighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Two forms of exercise that most easily arouse and are eagerly sought are sexual passion and fighting; a fight about sex outranks every other theme in breadth of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These motifs arouse strong, cross-cultural interest and are often blended. Political messaging often emphasizes the fighting motif (issues) because sex motif appears less in political imagery (except scandals, racial conflict). Use motifs carefully to mobilize broad attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense and struggle (narrative tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense... constitutes the difference between the masterpieces in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the pictures at the Rivoli or the Rialto Theatres; the motion picture draws people because it depicts unfolding events and possesses the element of struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience attention is held by depicting unfolding events, obstacles, antagonists, and problems. Techniques to add suspense: add an antagonist, add obstacles, emphasize questions in spectators' minds. Stories lacking suspense will fail to engage large audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability of distant/abstract situations into pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: A distant situation should be capable of translation into pictures in which the opportunity for identification is recognizable; otherwise it will interest only a few for a little while.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract or remote affairs must be rendered into concrete, pictorial scenes that allow personal identification; without this translation the content remains 'sights seen but not felt' and fails to motivate broad public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic beginning and romantic/happy ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular taste is to have the drama originate in a setting realistic enough to make identification plausible and to have it terminate in a setting romantic enough to be desirable; the true beginning and the happy ending are landmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences reject pure fantasy (no familiar foothold) and relentless realism (no enjoyment of defeat). Effective popular narratives balance believable starts with desirable, not implausible, resolutions to satisfy broad audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and persistence of stereotypes for commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers must adhere to the stereotypes that they find, or pay the price of frustrating expectation; stereotypes can be altered, but not in time to guarantee success when a film is released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High production costs and the need for instant, widespread popularity push managers and editors to rely on familiar stereotypes. Innovators may change stereotypes, but commercial producers usually protect investments by repeating recognized forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between pioneering innovation and commercial protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The men who do alter the stereotypes (pioneering artists and critics) are depressed and angered at managers and editors who protect their investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pioneers measure success by artistic standards and often resent commercial metrics (circulations, audiences). Producers should be aware of this tension: innovation risks commercial failure; imitation yields predictable mass appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pioneers crystallize collective feelings into new forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who 'catch on' (e.g., Sinclair Lewis) project what great numbers of other people were obscurely trying to say; they establish a new form which is then endlessly copied until it becomes a stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective innovators can articulate latent public sentiments and thereby create popular forms. Successful new forms will be imitated and eventually standardized, reducing their initial novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda formula: plausible beginning + utopian ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The skilful propagandist knows that while you must start with a plausible analysis, you must not keep on analyzing... he exhausts the interest in reality by a tolerably plausible beginning, and then stokes up energy for a long voyage by brandishing a passport to heaven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For persuasive political messaging: begin with a credible portrayal of present evils, then shift to grand promises of a better future to maintain energy and commitment. Avoid prolonged sober analysis that bores audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify which 'self' is being engaged (multifaceted self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-interest determines opinion, but the statement is not illuminating until we know which self out of many selects and directs the interest so conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People have multiple 'selves' (different roles/personas). Effective messaging must target the particular self that will be activated (e.g., patriot, homeowner, parent), because different selves produce very different responses to the same story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience heterogeneity increases abstraction and variation in response
rubrics_metrics.description: As the audience grows larger, the number of common words diminishes. Thus the common factors in the story become more abstract; the larger and more mixed the audience, the greater the variation in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing large, diverse publics, messages tend toward abstract, broadly shared symbols rather than detailed particulars. Expect greater divergence in individual recreations of the story as audience heterogeneity increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral education and preparation of characters for situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The preparation of characters for all the situations in which men may find themselves is one function of a moral education; moralists must either offer patterns for every phase of life or guarantee pupils will not face those phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public communicators and educators should recognize that people's behavior in public controversies depends on which character/persona is primed. Effective civic messaging or education must prepare audiences for likely moral dilemmas and roles they will assume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic determinism for predicting opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of property and economic position make a difference in opinion, but economic position alone does not determine what specific opinions people will hold; the economic determinist cannot tell which of a person's many relations produces a particular opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or analyzing political messages, do not assume simple economic categories predict responses. Investigate which social relations, roles, or experiences shape opinions rather than relying solely on class/economic labels.
